paras: The threatened lynching of R. O. Higgins took place in Yancey County, North Carolina, in late July 1888, when a lynching party pursued Higgins, a Black man accused of assaulting a ten-year-old Black girl. No report of Higgins's capture or fate appears in the coverage, which consisted of two brief items in out-of-state papers.

A special telegram from Raleigh printed in the Richmond Dispatch on 27 July 1888 stated that "a negro man named Higgins" had brutally, "perhaps fatally," injured a ten-year-old "colored girl named Connally" in Yancey County that week. The printed text says Higgins "assassinated" the girl, but because she is described as perhaps fatally hurt rather than killed, the word appears to be an error for "assaulted." Four days later the Atlanta Constitution gave his name as R. O. Higgins and said he had "brutally outraged" the girl "a few days ago."
Only the Atlanta item reported a response to the accusation: "A lynching party is after Higgins." It added that the girl's injuries were "thought to be fatal."
No later report of Higgins's arrest, capture, lynching or trial was found, and the coverage does not say whether the girl survived.

The case reached readers only as one-sentence notices in roundup columns. The Richmond Dispatch placed it among Raleigh state news under the deck "Brutal Outrage," next to items on the "Cross-White matter" and a farmer attacked by foxes. The Atlanta Constitution ran it under "Telegraph Tips," between a Chattanooga police case and a Nebraska train accident, and reported the lynching party without comment. Both papers stated the accusation as fact rather than as a charge, and neither named a source for it.
No account from a North Carolina paper was found.

A4 reports only that a lynching party was pursuing Higgins over an alleged assault; no report says he was caught or killed (A3, A4), so this is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.
Two separate telegraphic briefs agree that Higgins was accused of assaulting a ten-year-old girl in Yancey county (A3, A4), but only the Atlanta Constitution mentions the lynching party (A4).
